newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Philippine Navy hits back, says doing its best.
newsitem.headline: Philippine Navy hits back, says doing its best.

text.p: The Philippine navy on Friday hit back at charges that it was incapable against alleged Chinese intrusions into its waters and accusations of drug running, and said it had done its best with limited resources.
"We have recently got unsolicited (media) exposure on some cases...and we would like to clear these issues," information officer Lt. Commander Salvador Cuba told reporters.
The navy's public relations effort comes at a time when it is hoping to receive a major chunk of a $2-billion-armed forces modernisation programme spread over five years.

At a news conference ahead of it's 99th aniversary celebrations next week, navy chief Vice Admiral Eduardo Santos said modernisation was essential if the navy was to guard the 7,100 islands of this archipelago nation.
The Philippines recently protested that three Chinese warships had intruded into an area in the Spratlys islands claimed by Manila.
The Spratlys islands in the South China Sea are believed to be rich in oil and are claimed wholly or in part by Vietnam, Taiwan, the Philippines, Malaysia, Brunei and China.
Aside from a formal protest to Beijing, the Philippines has done nothing except said it would use diplomacy.
The government's stand focused attention on the ill-equipped navy, and local newspapers said Manila had no other choice but to threaten with words rather than guns.
"I still subscribe to the use of diplomacy and the use of economics to come out with an acceptable understanding of how we will be able to utilise the (Spratlys) area," Santos said.
"I would not propose an armed encounter...we wouldn't want to be involved, but if push comes to shove, then we will do our job," he said.
Santos said the navy was in urgent need of new ships, but then, "where do you use your money -- to buy rice or rifles? We cannot impose on our policy makers to buy only rifles."
He said under the modernisation programme, the navy would acquire three new offshore patrol vessels.
Separately, it is also buying three British vessels based in Hong Kong that would be put out of commission after the colony is handed back to China at midnight on June 30, he said.

The further allocation of money from the $2-billion-fund would depend on the Philippine Congress, which could be swayed by another recent allegation that some naval officers were involved in drug running.

"That's completely absurd. I conducted some investigations and I found nothing that would lead to even a tinge of veracity of the statement that the vessel was involved in drug trafficking," Commander Tirso Danga, chief of naval intelligence, told Reuters on board the ship allegedly involved in the crime.
